{{Short description|Inequalities in number theory and matrix theory}}
{{about|Weyl's inequality in linear algebra|Weyl's inequality in number theory|Weyl's inequality (number theory)}}

In [[linear algebra]], '''Weyl's inequality''' is a theorem about the changes to [[eigenvalues]] of a [[Hermitian matrix]] that is perturbed.  It can be used to estimate the eigenvalues of a perturbed Hermitian matrix. 

==Weyl's inequality about perturbation==

Let <math display="inline">A,B</math> be Hermitian on [[inner product space]] <math display="inline">V</math> with dimension <math display="inline">n</math>, with spectrum ordered in descending order <math display="inline">\lambda_1 \geq ... \geq \lambda_n</math>. Note that these eigenvalues can be ordered, because they are real (as eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices).<ref name=":0" />

{{Math theorem|name=Weyl inequality|note=|math_statement=
Let <math display="inline">A,B</math> be <math display="inline">n\times n</math> Hermitian matrices, and let <math display="inline">1 \leq i,j \le n</math> be integers.
If <math display="inline">i+j \leq n+1</math>, then
<math display="block">\lambda_{i+j-1}(A+B) \leq \lambda_i(A)+\lambda_j(B).</math>
If <math display="inline"> n < i+j</math>, then 
<math display="block">\lambda_i(A)+\lambda_j(B) \leq \lambda_{i+j-n}(A+B).</math>
}}
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 

By the [[min-max theorem]], it suffices to show that any <math display="inline">W \subset V</math> with dimension <math display="inline">i+j-1</math>, there exists a unit vector <math display="inline">w</math> such that <math display="inline">\langle w, (A+B)w\rangle \leq \lambda_i(A) + \lambda_j(B)</math>.

By the min-max principle, there exists some <math display="inline">W_A</math> with codimension <math display="inline">(i-1)</math>, such that <math display="block">\lambda_i(A) = \max_{x\in W_A; \|x\|=1}\langle x, Ax\rangle</math> Similarly, there exists such a <math display="inline">W_B</math> with codimension <math display="inline">j-1</math>. Now <math display="inline">W_A \cap W_B</math> has codimension <math display="inline">\leq i+j-2</math>, so it has nontrivial intersection with <math display="inline">W</math>. Let <math display="inline">w \in W \cap W_A \cap W_B</math>, and we have the desired vector.

The second one is a corollary of the first, by taking the negative.
}}

Weyl's inequality states that the spectrum of Hermitian matrices is stable under perturbation. Specifically, we have:<ref name=":0" />

{{Math theorem|name=Corollary (Spectral stability)|note=|math_statement= 
<math display="block">\lambda_k(A+B) - \lambda_k(A) \in [\lambda_n(B), \lambda_1(B)]</math> 
<math display="block">|\lambda_k(A+B) - \lambda_k(A)| \leq \|B\|_{op}</math> where<br />
<math display="block">\|B\|_{op} = \max(|\lambda_1(B)|, |\lambda_n(B)|)</math> is the operator norm.
}}

In jargon, it says that <math>\lambda_k</math> is [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz-continuous]] on the space of Hermitian matrices with [[operator norm]].

==Weyl's inequality between eigenvalues and singular values ==
Let <math>A \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}</math> have singular values <math>\sigma_1(A) \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_n(A) \geq 0</math> and eigenvalues ordered so that <math>|\lambda_1(A)| \geq \cdots \geq |\lambda_n(A)|</math>. Then

:<math> |\lambda_1(A) \cdots \lambda_k(A)| \leq \sigma_1(A) \cdots \sigma_k(A)</math>

For <math>k = 1, \ldots, n</math>, with equality for <math>k=n</math>.
<ref>Roger A. Horn, and Charles R. Johnson Topics in Matrix Analysis. Cambridge, 1st Edition, 1991. p.171</ref>

==Applications==

=== Estimating perturbations of the spectrum ===

Let Hermitian matrices <math>M</math> and <math>N</math> differ by a matrix <math>R</math>. Assume that <math>R</math> is small in the sense that its spectral norm satisfies <math>\|R\|_2 \le \epsilon</math> for some small <math>\epsilon>0</math>. Then it follows that all the eigenvalues of <math>R</math> are bounded in absolute value by <math>\epsilon</math>. Applying Weyl's inequality, it follows that the spectra of the Hermitian matrices ''M'' and ''N'' are close in the sense that<ref>
Weyl, Hermann. [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01456804 "Das asymptotische Verteilungsgesetz der Eigenwerte linearer partieller Differentialgleichungen (mit einer Anwendung auf die Theorie der Hohlraumstrahlung)."] Mathematische Annalen 71, no. 4 (1912): 441-479.</ref>

:<math>|\mu_i - \nu_i| \le \epsilon \qquad \forall i=1,\ldots,n.</math>

Note, however, that this [[eigenvalue perturbation]] bound is generally false for non-Hermitian matrices (or more accurately, for non-normal matrices). For a [[counterexample]], let <math>t>0</math> be arbitrarily small, and consider  
:<math>M = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1/t^2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad N = M + R = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1/t^2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad R = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.</math>
whose eigenvalues <math>\mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0</math> and <math>\nu_1 = +1/t, \nu_2 = -1/t</math> do not satisfy <math>|\mu_i - \nu_i| \le \|R\|_2 = 1</math>.

=== Weyl's inequality for singular values ===
Let <math>M</math> be a <math>p \times n</math> matrix with <math>1 \le p \le n</math>. Its [[singular value]]s <math>\sigma_k(M)</math> are the <math>p</math> positive eigenvalues of the <math>(p+n) \times (p+n)</math> Hermitian [[augmented matrix]]

:<math>\begin{bmatrix} 0 & M \\ M^* & 0 \end{bmatrix}.</math>

Therefore, Weyl's eigenvalue perturbation inequality for Hermitian matrices extends naturally to perturbation of singular values.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|last1=Tao|first1=Terence|title=254A, Notes 3a: Eigenvalues and sums of Hermitian matrices|url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/01/12/254a-notes-3a-eigenvalues-and-sums-of-hermitian-matrices/|website=Terence Tao's blog|accessdate=25 May 2015|date=2010-01-13}}</ref> This result gives the bound for the perturbation in the singular values of a matrix <math>M</math> due to an additive perturbation <math>\Delta</math>:
:<math>|\sigma_k(M+\Delta) - \sigma_k(M)| \le \sigma_1(\Delta)</math>
where we note that the largest singular value <math>\sigma_1(\Delta)</math> coincides with the spectral norm <math>\|\Delta\|_2</math>.
